I don't think you're right about that. Long before space photos existed, people had evidence the Earth was round. Ships disappear hull-first over the horizon. The Earth casts a curved shadow on the Moon during lunar eclipses. Travelers see different stars as they go north or south. Eratosthenes measured the Earth's circumference around 240 BC using shadow lengths in two cities. You can check most of this yourself without trusting NASA. If a specific piece of evidence convinced you otherwise, tell me what it is and I'll look at it.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's a mix of all the colors. Each color is a wave, and blue has shorter waves than red. When sunlight hits the air, the tiny molecules of nitrogen and oxygen bounce light around in all directions. They're much better at bouncing short waves than long ones, about five times better for blue than for red. So blue light gets scattered all over the sky, and wherever you look, some of it is coming toward you. Violet waves are even shorter, so you might ask why the sky isn't violet. The sun gives off less violet, and your eyes are less sensitive to it. At sunset, light travels through much more air to reach you. Most of the blue gets scattered away before it arrives, and the reds and oranges are what's left.
